title: Canada's Carney Mocks Trump Over Conspiracy Claims
excerpt: Since Trump returned to the Oval Office for a second term, relations between the U.S. and Canada have become increasingly strained.
content_html:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney took a swipe at U.S. President Donald Trump when a teleprompter malfunctioned in the middle of his on-camera speech.

During a housing policy news briefing at a construction site in Toronto on Wednesday, Carney was speaking in French before he abruptly stopped, telling the crowd in English: “I would now like to inform you that the teleprompter has ceased to function. Unlike a certain world leader, I do not view this as a conspiracy.”

Carney laughed, along with the audience, as he delivered the quip, before launching back into the French-language portion of his speech.  

The remark appeared to reference Trump's claims of “sabotage” after a teleprompter malfunctioned during his address at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last September.

“I don’t mind making this speech without a teleprompter, because the teleprompter is not working,” Trump had said on stage. “I can only say that whoever’s operating this teleprompter is in big trouble.”

The incident came after Trump and his wife, First Lady Melania, encountered a stalled escalator en route to the main speaking hall.

“This wasn’t a coincidence, this was triple sabotage at the U.N. They ought to be ashamed of themselves. I’m sending a copy of this letter to the Secretary General, and I demand an immediate investigation,” he said after the event, insisting there had also been sound issues in the auditorium.

Trump has yet to publicly respond to Carney referencing the teleprompter incident, but he did continue his criticism of Canada during his own speech on Wednesday afternoon.

Addressing a crowd at the Red Rock Casino Resort in Las Vegas, Nevada, Trump touted his economic and immigration policies ahead of the crucial November midterm elections.

Referencing his controversial approach to tariffs, Trump said: “I love tariffs, right? Because we've been screwed by tariffs used against us for years. By China, by Japan, by South Korea, by Germany, by everybody, by Canada.”

Going on to insult his northern neighbors, the President continued: “Canada’s nasty. They are, they’re nasty. I love the people, but they’re nasty, nasty leadership.”

Carney laughed on Thursday when a reporter asked him about Trump's use of the word "nasty" in reference to Canada, and centered his response by reflecting on the ongoing trade talks.

"Yes, it's a tough negotiation. You can change the adjective and say 'nasty,' but for ​Canada it's ​a question ⁠of Canadian jobs, it's a question of the future of Canadian enterprises," he said. "Whatever adjective is used, yes, we're standing up for Canadian workers, for Canadian businesses as we always have from the start."

The widening rift between Carney and Trump

Since Trump returned to the Oval Office for a second term, relations between the two countries have become increasingly strained, partly due to a long-standing row over trade.

Canada imposed tariffs on some vehicle imports from the U.S. in 2025 amid a trade war sparked by Trump’s global tariffs, the majority of which were struck down by a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year.

In early July, tensions came to a head once more when the U.S. declined to renew the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

Toward the end of the month, Trump announced a 50% tariff hike on Canadian goods, with the levies set to come into effect on Aug. 19.

In an April 2025 interview with TIME, Trump denied he was “trolling” when talking about annexation. “We’re taking care of their military. We're taking care of every aspect of their lives… We don't need anything from Canada. And I say the only way this thing really works is for Canada to become a state,” he said.

Carney has strongly pushed back against the rhetoric, stressing Canada's sovereignty is “not for sale.”

Other Canadian officials have also vocalized their opposition, with Ontario Premier Doug Ford insisting: “Canada will never be the 51st state.” 

Meanwhile, Canada has been battling a series of major summer wildfires, with smoke drifting into parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States.

Trump seized on the crisis to again criticize Canada's leadership, vowing to hold the country “responsible” on account of the U.S. being “unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted, and unhealthy air.”

When asked whether he had decided on a penalty for Canada over the wildfire smoke, Trump told reporters on Aug. 2: “I have, yeah. You’ll find out about it.” He did not elaborate further.

How a bridge became a symbol of U.S.-Canada tensions

One symbol of the deteriorating relationship is the Gordie Howe International Bridge. The construction and collaboration involved in the newly-opened bridge, which connects Detroit, Michigan, to Windsor, Ontario, was plagued with difficulties. 

Trump, in February, threatened to block the bridge's opening, complaining that the infrastructure had been built with “virtually no U.S. content” and demanding compensation.

Tensions erupted after the White House announced a 50% hike on certain Canadian goods on July 20, in response to what it insisted was Canada’s “discriminatory treatment” of American products.

"In light of trade action threatened by the United States, it would be inappropriate to proceed with a celebratory event between the two countries,” Jenna Ghassabeh, a spokesperson for Canadian Infrastructure Minister Gregor Robertson, told TIME in an emailed statement ahead of the event.

At the ceremony, Ford—who was dressed in a Team Canada jersey in honor of prolific Canadian ice hockey player Gordie Howe—said "Canada has never been more united.” He vowed that “Ontario will be ready to respond to any new American tariffs [and] will not back down and will negotiate from a position of strength."

Trump called out Canada’s decision to “disinvite” the U.S. officials, but said he was ultimately fine about the move “considering they [Canada] are paying substantial tariffs to the United States.”

content_html_zh:
加拿大总理马克·卡尼在美国总统唐纳德·特朗普在镜头前演讲时提词器出现故障，对他进行了猛烈抨击。

周三，在多伦多一处建筑工地举行的住房政策新闻发布会上，卡尼用法语讲话，然后突然停下来，用英语告诉人群：“我现在想通知你们，提词器已经停止工作。 与某个世界领导人不同，我不认为这是一个阴谋。”

卡尼在发表这句俏皮话时和观众一起笑了，然后又开始讲法语部分。

这番话似乎是指特朗普去年 9 月在纽约联合国大会发表演讲时提词器发生故障后所声称的“破坏行为”。

“我不介意在没有提词器的情况下发表演讲，因为提词器不起作用，”特朗普在台上说道。 “我只能说，无论是谁操作这个提词器，都有大麻烦了。”

事件发生之前，特朗普和他的妻子第一夫人梅拉尼娅在前往主演讲厅的途中遇到了一辆停住的自动扶梯。

“这不是巧合，这是对联合国的三重破坏。 他们应该为自己感到羞耻。 我正在向秘书长发送这封信的副本，我要求立即进行调查，”他在活动结束后说道，并坚称礼堂中也存在声音问题。

特朗普尚未公开回应卡尼提到的提词器事件，但他在周三下午的演讲中确实继续批评加拿大。

特朗普在内华达州拉斯维加斯红岩赌场度假村向人群发表讲话，在关键的 11 月中期选举之前宣传他的经济和移民政策。

特朗普在谈到他备受争议的关税方法时表示：“我喜欢关税，对吧？ 因为多年来我们一直被针对我们的关税所困扰。 中国、日本、韩国、德国、所有人、加拿大。”

总统继续侮辱他的北方邻国：“加拿大很肮脏。 他们是，他们很讨厌。 我爱这里的人，但他们的领导能力非常非常恶劣。”

周四，当一名记者问及特朗普在提到加拿大时使用“令人讨厌”一词时，卡尼笑了，并通过反思正在进行的贸易谈判来集中回答。

“是的，这是一场艰难的谈判。 你可以换个形容词，说‘令人讨厌’，但对加拿大来说，这是一个加拿大就业的问题，这是一个加拿大企业未来的问题，”他说。 “无论使用什么形容词，是的，我们从一开始就一直在为加拿大工人、加拿大企业挺身而出。”

卡尼和特朗普之间的分歧日益扩大

自特朗普重返椭圆形办公室连任以来，两国关系日益紧张，部分原因是长期存在的贸易争端。

在特朗普全球关税引发的贸易战中，加拿大于 2025 年对部分从美国进口的汽车征收关税，其中大部分关税已被最高法院今年早些时候的一项裁决推翻。

7月初，当美国拒绝续签美墨加协议时，紧张局势再次达到顶峰。

月底，特朗普宣布对加拿大商品加征 50% 的关税，并于 8 月 19 日生效。

在 2025 年 4 月接受《时代》杂志采访时，特朗普否认自己在谈论吞并问题时“恶搞”。 “我们正在照顾他们的军队。 我们正在照顾他们生活的方方面面...... 我们不需要来自加拿大的任何东西。 我说，这件事真正起作用的唯一方法就是让加拿大成为一个州，”他说。

卡尼强烈反驳了这种言论，强调加拿大的主权“是非卖品”。

其他加拿大官员也表达了反对意见，安大略省省长道格·福特坚称：“加拿大永远不会成为第 51 个州。”

与此同时，加拿大一直在与一系列夏季重大野火作斗争，烟雾飘入美国东北部和中西部部分地区。

特朗普利用这场危机再次批评加拿大的领导层，并发誓要让加拿大承担“责任”，因为美国“不必要地受到肮脏、污染和不健康的空气的入侵”。

当被问及是否已决定就山火烟雾对加拿大进行处罚时，特朗普于 8 月 2 日告诉记者：“我已经决定了，是的。 你会知道的。” 他没有进一步说明。

一座桥梁如何成为美加紧张局势的象征

戈迪·豪国际大桥是两国关系恶化的象征之一。 这座连接密歇根州底特律和安大略省温莎的新大桥的建设和协作遇到了困难。

特朗普在二月份威胁要阻止这座桥的开放，抱怨该基础设施的建设“几乎没有美国成分”，并要求赔偿。

7月20日，白宫宣布对某些加拿大商品加价50%，以回应其坚称加拿大对美国产品的“歧视性待遇”，随后紧张局势爆发。

加拿大基础设施部长格雷戈尔·罗伯逊 (Gregor Robertson) 发言人珍娜·加萨贝 (Jenna Ghassabeh) 在活动前通过电子邮件发表的声明中告诉《时代》杂志：“鉴于美国威胁采取贸易行动，两国之间继续举办庆祝活动是不合适的。”

在仪式上，福特身穿加拿大队球衣，以纪念多产的加拿大冰球运动员戈迪·豪（Gordie Howe），他说：“加拿大从未如此团结。” 他发誓，“安大略省将准备好应对任何新的美国关税，并且不会退缩，并将以强势地位进行谈判。”

特朗普对加拿大“取消邀请”美国官员的决定表示不满，但表示他最终对此举没有意见，“考虑到他们（加拿大）正在向美国支付大量关税”。
